plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked Nociception, Spinal Gate Control & Endogenous Opioid Analgesia chart from Charles Sherrington (1906 The Integrative Action of the Nervous System), Henry Beecher (1946 Ann. Surg. 123: 96–105 & 1955 JAMA 159: 1602–1606), Ronald Melzack & Patrick Wall (19 November 1965 Science 150: 971–979), Candace Pert & Solomon Snyder (9 March 1973 Science 179: 1011–1014), and John Hughes & Hans Kosterlitz (18 December 1975 Nature 258: 577–579) shows 1) Peripheral A-delta (5–30 m/s) and C-fibre (0.5–2 m/s) nociceptors; 2) Spinal dorsal horn substantia gelatinosa (SG) inhibitory gate closed by fast A-beta touch fibres (35–75 m/s); and 3) Descending brainstem analgesia releasing endogenous enkephalins/endorphins onto mu/delta opioid receptors.

teach_overlay.detail: Inked Melzack & Wall (1965) nerve conduction velocity comparison (A-beta touch fibres 35–75 m/s vs A-delta sharp pain 5–30 m/s vs C-fibre throbbing pain 0.5–2 m/s) & spinal dorsal horn Gate Control circuit on period paper
teach_overlay.scale: your touch nerves race up to your spine at seventy-five metres per second — as fast as an express train — while your throbbing pain nerves crawl at just one metre per second, a walking pace, so rubbing a bumped shin lets the touch signals reach your spinal cord first and slam the gate shut before the pain arrives
